specPoints.text: understand that fertilisation involves the fusion of a male and female gamete to produce a zygote that undergoes cell division and develops into an embryo

primer.text: Every human starts as a single cell built from two half-cells. This note introduces the gametes — sperm and ovum — with the adaptations that help each one win its race or feed its passenger, then follows fertilisation from the oviduct meeting to the zygote's first mitotic divisions toward an embryo.

lessons.title: The Sex Cells and Their Adaptations
lessons.opening: Gametes are the sex cells made by meiosis, holding half the normal chromosome count: sperm swim with a tail and burn mitochondrial fuel, while the ovum sits rich in cytoplasm packed with energy stores for the early embryo.
keyPoints: Gametes are sex cells produced by meiosis: sperm and ovum in animals, pollen nucleus and ovum in plants.
Gametes contain half the number of chromosomes of normal body cells — 23 in human gametes.
Sperm have a tail to propel them and mitochondria supplying energy for movement.
Egg cells hold energy stores in their cytoplasm to support early embryo development.

low.restatement: Sperm travel light with a tail and an engine; eggs stay put but carry a packed lunch for the embryo.
low.analogy: A motorcycle courier racing to a delivery, and a depot stocked for the month after arrival.
low.examPointer: Quote the haploid count — 23 in humans — and tie each adaptation to its function.

medium.restatement: Meiosis halves the chromosome set so fertilisation can restore it; the tail and mitochondria exist because reaching the ovum is a competition, while the cytoplasmic reserves exist because the zygote must grow before any placenta supplies it.
medium.analogy: One cell arrives as a swimmer, the other waits as a supply drop.
medium.examPointer: Link adaptation to chance of successful fertilisation — that phrase earns the marks.

check.stem: How many chromosomes does a human gamete carry?

options.text: 23, half the number in body cells
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
46 is the diploid body-cell number; gametes halve it.
Nothing doubles to 92 at meiosis.
Gametes hold 23 singles, not 23 pairs.

check.stem: Which adaptation helps a sperm cell reach the ovum?

options.text: A tail that propels it, powered by mitochondria
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: A thick energy store in its cytoplasm
options.explanation: Energy stores belong to the egg cell.

options.text: A hard coat that blocks rivals
options.explanation: No taught sperm coat blocks rivals.

options.text: Cilia that sweep it down the oviduct
options.explanation: Cilia line the oviduct wall; the sperm swims itself.

check.stem: Why does the ovum carry energy stores in its cytoplasm?

options.text: To support the early embryo's development before other nutrition arrives
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
The ovum does not swim.
The sperm brings its own mitochondria.
Lining growth is hormonal, not cytoplasmic.

check.stem: Which cells are produced by meiosis?

options.text: The gametes — sperm and ovum in animals, pollen nucleus and ovum in plants
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Body cells divide by mitosis.
The zygote divides by mitosis, not meiosis.

options.text: The cells of the uterine lining
options.explanation: Lining cells are ordinary diploid body cells.

check.stem: A lab images two cells: one tiny with a long tail, one large with dense cytoplasm. What has been photographed?

options.text: A sperm and an ovum — the two human gametes
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Body cells show neither tails nor gamete cytoplasm.
A zygote has fused nuclei and no tail.

options.text: A pollen grain and a seed
options.explanation: Seeds and pollen are plant structures, not human cells.

check.stem: State the chromosome number in a human gamete and say how it compares with body cells.
check.modelAnswer: A human gamete carries 23 chromosomes, half the number found in normal body cells.

check.stem: Name the two adaptations of a sperm cell mentioned in the lesson.
check.modelAnswer: A sperm has a tail to propel it and mitochondria to provide energy for that movement.

check.stem: Explain why gametes must be produced by meiosis rather than mitosis.
check.modelAnswer: Meiosis halves the chromosome number so that fertilisation restores the full count; mitotic gametes would produce a zygote with double the normal chromosomes.

check.stem: A new fertility treatment selects sperm with the strongest swimming. Name the structure being assessed and its energy supplier.
check.modelAnswer: The structure assessed is the tail, and its movement is powered by mitochondria supplying energy.

lessons.title: Fertilisation and the First Divisions
lessons.opening: Fertilisation is the fusion of a male and a female gamete into a zygote: sperm deposited near the cervix swim up, meet the egg in the oviduct, and the restored 46-chromosome cell divides by mitosis into a specialised embryo.
keyPoints: Fertilisation is the fusion of a male gamete and a female gamete to produce a zygote.
In humans the sperm meets the egg in the oviduct, typically one to two days after ovulation.
The zygote holds the full 46 chromosomes, half from each parent.
The zygote divides by mitosis and its cells specialise into an embryo's body tissues.

low.restatement: Two half-cells fuse into one whole cell, which then copies itself repeatedly and specialises into an embryo.
low.analogy: Two half-sheets of paper joined into one full sheet, then photocopied into a growing stack.
low.examPointer: Use the word fusion and name the zygote as the product — both are on the spec line.

medium.restatement: The oviduct meeting point matters because the egg is short-lived; after fusion, mitosis copies the restored genome so every descendant cell carries the full 46, and differentiation then assigns those copies to tissue jobs.
medium.analogy: Two keys cut to half a lock each click together and open the safe; then the safe starts printing itself.
medium.examPointer: Say mitosis for the divisions after fusion — meiosis made the gametes, mitosis grows the embryo.

options.text: The fusion of a male gamete and a female gamete to produce a zygote
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: The division of a zygote into an embryo
options.explanation: That follows fertilisation; it is not fertilisation itself.

options.text: The release of an egg from the ovary
options.explanation: That is ovulation.

options.text: The growth of the uterine lining
options.explanation: Lining growth prepares implantation, not fusion.

check.stem: Where in the human female does fertilisation usually happen?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
The uterus hosts implantation; the oviduct hosts fusion.
The ovary releases the egg but does not host fertilisation.
Sperm are deposited near the vagina's top; fusion happens higher up.

check.stem: How many chromosomes does a human zygote hold, and from where?

options.text: 46 — half from the father and half from the mother
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
23 is the gamete count; the zygote restores 46.
Both parents contribute half each.
Fusion adds 23 to 23, not doubles 46.

check.stem: Which type of cell division turns the zygote into a many-celled embryo?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Meiosis made the gametes; it does not grow the embryo.
Fusion is the fertilisation event, not a division.
Specialisation follows; the copying division is mitosis.

check.stem: After fertilisation, some zygote descendant cells become muscle while others become nerve. What happened?

options.text: The cells specialised to perform specific functions during embryo development
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Meiosis does not run in the embryo's tissues.

options.text: The cells fused with new gametes
options.explanation: No further gametes join the embryo.
All descendant cells keep the same 46.

check.stem: State the event that occurs in the oviduct one to two days after ovulation if sperm are present.
check.modelAnswer: Fertilisation occurs in the oviduct when a sperm meets the egg, typically one to two days after ovulation.

check.stem: State what a zygote divides by and what it develops into.
check.modelAnswer: The zygote divides by mitosis and develops into an embryo.

check.stem: Explain why a zygote contains 46 chromosomes when each gamete contained only 23.
check.modelAnswer: Fertilisation fuses two gametes, so the 23 chromosomes from the sperm and the 23 from the egg combine to give the full 46.

check.stem: A couple conceive naturally. State the chromosome source split in their child's body cells.
check.modelAnswer: Every body cell carries 46 chromosomes, with 23 inherited from the father and 23 from the mother.

glossary.definition: A sex cell carrying half the normal chromosome number, produced by meiosis.
The single cell formed when a male and female gamete fuse at fertilisation.
The tube between ovary and uterus where fertilisation usually occurs.
The early stage of development formed as the zygote divides by mitosis.
